title_en: The Macro Implications of the Blue Tsunami
title_zh: 蓝色海啸的宏观影响：Skanda Amarnath（Employed America）解读民主党横扫
subtitle_zh: 民主党拿下国会与 Texas 一夜变蓝，对 Fed、关税与 AI 数据中心意味着什么
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 请来 Employed America 执行董事 Skanda Amarnath，解读民主党「蓝色海啸」（blue tsunami）——不仅拿下众议院，还赢下悬念更大的参议院，Texas 出现接近两位数摇摆——的宏观含义。Amarnath 强调参议院的结构性意义：它决定谁能进最高法院与 Fed 理事会，长期是 GOP 的优势所在（看州数而非人数，Kansas、Iowa 等人口份额下降的农业州权重偏高），而这次让民主党看到持续竞争的可能。节目复盘选前预期落空：Bank of America 的 Michael Hartnett 曾预测民主党胜选会令 S&P 500 跌 10%，结果指数反而涨约 1.5%，但在 Texas 重金布局的 SpaceX、Tesla 及部分新云服务商被砸。三人讨论 Fed 理事提名与 Jay Powell 可能留任至 2028 年初带来的空缺填补难题、AI 数据中心资本开支（CapEx）遇上的邻避主义（NIMBYism）、California 财富税公投失败，以及 Musk 从 DOGE 经历中的巨大资金浪费——引用 John Arnold「政治捐献才是原版的财富税」。Amarnath 还观察到若 AI CapEx 放缓、利率下行，疲软的房地产等板块反而有更多繁荣空间，并强调在版图剧变中保持认知谦逊、实时更新先验。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio. News. Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Lodge Podcast. I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客、广播、新闻。大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客，我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: Well, Tracy, I'm glad we did that episode that came out Tuesday with Nate Silver because he did go on record as like there's going to be a blue wave. And it turns out that was actually just this. It was correct in some sense, depending on how you measure wave. But it was just like, you know, it was a tsunami. Yeah. Maybe like maybe bigger than a tsunami.
turns.zh: Tracy，我真庆幸我们做了周二播出去的那一期跟 Nate Silver 的节目，因为他确实公开说过会有一场蓝色浪潮（blue wave）。结果证明这个判断是对的——从某种角度讲是对的，取决于你怎么定义'浪潮'。但你知道，这根本就是一场海啸（tsunami）。是啊，说不定比海啸还猛。

turns.en: It was seismic, for sure. So as everyone knows by now, the Democrats took both the House and the Senate. Going into it, as we discussed with Nate, I think most people thought there was a good chance they were going to take control of Congress, right?
turns.zh: 这肯定是地震级的。所以现在大家都知道了，民主党拿下了众议院和参议院。选前我们跟 Nate 讨论的时候，我想大多数人都觉得民主党很有希望控制国会，对吧？

turns.en: The House was seen as a lock.
turns.zh: 众议院被认为是稳赢的。

turns.en: The House was seen as a lock. But the big question was the Senate, which was like more of a coin flip. But Nate... Nate thought the Senate was actually looking pretty good.
turns.zh: 众议院被认为是稳赢的。但真正悬念大的是参议院，那更像是抛硬币。不过 Nate……Nate 觉得参议院那边对民主党其实形势相当不错。

turns.en: For the Democrats.
turns.zh: 对民主党来说。

turns.en: He was right.
turns.zh: 他说对了。

turns.en: He pushed back. I remember you're like, so the Senate is more of a coin flip. He's like, no, it's not. It feels like a coin flip in your head. But he was like, they just say it's on a coin flip. Turned out it was nothing close to. Turned out it was nothing close to a coin flip.
turns.zh: 他当时反驳过来。我记得你说'参议院更像抛硬币'，他就说'不，不是。感觉像抛硬币只是你脑子里的感觉。'他说他们只是嘴上说是抛硬币。结果证明根本不是抛硬币，差得远。

turns.en: So obviously the big question now for both markets and the economy is what changes under Democrat control? What can Trump still do? Of course, he posted that photo of his veto hat on Truth Social.
turns.zh: 所以显然，现在对市场和经济来说最大的问题是：民主党掌控之后会有什么变化？Trump 还能做什么？当然，他在 Truth Social 上发了他戴着那顶'否决帽'（veto hat）的照片。

turns.en: You saw that, right?
turns.zh: 你看到那个了吧？

turns.en: So the implication is that he can veto anything that the Democrats try to push through. He still has a lot of executive order power for things like tariffs. So how much does this really change? The other thing... So the expectation going in to the midterms was that if Democrats actually win, this would be terrible for stocks, right? I know. And you saw Michael Hartnett from Bank of America. He said he thought the S & P 500 could fall 10% if Democrats win. Yeah, apparently, which turned out to be wrong because we saw a Democratic victory. And I think the S & P 500 was up like one and a half percent yesterday.
turns.zh: 言下之意就是，民主党想推什么他都可以否决。他在关税这些事情上还有大量的行政令（executive order）权力。所以这到底能改变多少？另一件事……选前的预期是，如果民主党真的赢了，这对股市会是灾难，对吧？我知道。你也看到 Bank of America 的 Michael Hartnett，他说他觉得如果民主党赢了，S&P 500 可能会跌 10%。是的，据说是这样，结果证明是错的，因为我们看到民主党胜选，而昨天 S&P 500 大概涨了 1.5%。

turns.en: Yeah, it was. But OK, but now we're recording this November 5th.
turns.zh: 对，是涨了。但好，我们现在是在 11 月 5 日录这期。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And it's 938 and the NASDAQ is getting hammered. So what is true, and it was like isolated in the day after like SpaceX and Tesla, which have as companies put a lot of money, both in Texas and red Texas specifically, they got hit pretty hard. Some of these new clouds that have like dreams of expanding their footprint, et cetera, got hit pretty hard. Now it was kind of a mix. I don't know. Anyway, the other thing, by the way, that is relevant of course, is any future. Fed governors in our world.
turns.zh: 现在是 9 点 38 分，NASDAQ 正被狠砸。所以真实情况是——昨天跌得比较集中的是像 SpaceX 和 Tesla 这种公司，它们在 Texas——特别是红的 Texas——砸了很多钱进去，被砸得挺惨。一些本来还想扩张地盘的新云服务商也被砸得挺惨。所以昨天是个混合行情，我也不知道。总之，另一件相关的事当然是——未来的 Fed 理事。在我们的世界里……

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: In our world, you know, if there are any Fed governor appointments coming up. Anyway, to talk about all this, very excited to say, welcoming back to the show, perfect guest, because he knows both worlds. Skanda Amarnath, Executive Director of Employee America. Actually, all three worlds, because in addition to knowing macro and politics, You're also sort of a markets junkie, but you don't really talk about that as much publicly.
turns.zh: 在我们的世界里，你知道，如果接下来还有 Fed 理事要提名。总之，为了聊所有这些，我非常高兴地说，欢迎回到节目，一位完美的嘉宾，因为他同时懂这两个世界——Skanda Amarnath，Employed America 的执行董事。其实是三个世界都懂，因为除了宏观和政治，你还算是个市场痴迷者，只是你公开场合不太聊这个。

turns.en: We'll get you to do equity recommendations.
turns.zh: 我们会让你做点股票推荐的。

turns.en: We'll get Skanda's five lockpicks for Q4. No, but for real, let's stick just with the politics for a second. We're recording this November 5th, so we all know what happened. But are there any dimensions of the earthquake tidal wave extinction level event for the GOP that stand out for you in some way? I mean, I think people were missing.
turns.zh: 我们会拿到 Skanda 四季度的五个精选股。不，说正经的，我们先聊聊政治。我们是在 11 月 5 日录的，所以大家都知道发生了什么。但对 GOP 来说这场地震、海啸、灭绝级事件，有没有哪个维度让你特别印象深刻？我觉得大家伙儿都错过了……

turns.en: Yeah, I think that the Senate itself, this is more structural, just really matters for the American government. It is sort of the institution that shapes who serves on the Supreme Court. It's the institution that shapes who serves on the Fed board. And for a long time, there's been a pretty structural advantage for the GOP.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得参议院本身——这更偏结构性——对美国政府真的很重要。它是决定谁能进最高法院的机构，也是决定谁能进 Fed 理事会的机构。长期以来，GOP 在参议院一直有一个相当结构性的优势。

turns.en: In the Senate.
turns.zh: 在参议院。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And maybe that advantage is still true and this blue tsunami will be a one-off. But I think you at least see for Democrats, there is a path ahead for how they could sustainably Stay competitive in the Senate. That's not reaching to get to 50 to 51 votes. I think that can change a lot of different things.
turns.zh: 也许这个优势依然存在，这场蓝色海啸只是一次性的。但我觉得至少对民主党来说，前面有一条路，让他们可以在参议院持续保持竞争力。这不是硬凑到 50 或 51 票的问题。我觉得这能改变很多东西。

turns.en: And the structural advantage for the GOP and the Senate comes down to the fact that if you take a state like Kansas or Iowa or whatever, they haven't seen a lot of population growth. Their share of like is outside. But they still get two votes, just like New York. And if there's ever a time when there's down to like 100 people left in Wyoming, they're probably the assumption is going to be Republicans. And they're going to have infinitely more influence over the rest of the country than New York.
turns.zh: GOP 在参议院的结构性优势归根结底在于：像 Kansas 或 Iowa 之类的州，人口没怎么增长，他们的人口份额在下降，但他们还是有兩票，跟 New York 一样。如果哪一天 Wyoming 只剩下 100 个人，那大概率也是共和党人，而他们对全国的影响力就会远远超过 New York。

turns.en: The Senate is about the number of states, not the number of people.
turns.zh: 参议院看的是州的数量，不是人的数量。

turns.en: And Corrin doesn't vote, as they say.
turns.zh: 而且就像大家说的，'玉米不会投票'。

turns.en: Except in the Midwest. I would say what Bob Dole had some quote about basically. way more ag states than there are any other kind of state. And that's going to always count more. I think that has some implications for sort of how kind of power is shaped from here. For Democrats, there's also just a sense of, oh, this was actually possible. I don't think Democrats expected to win in South Carolina unless they were in the Annie Andrews campaign, maybe. I don't think they expected to win in Mississippi. And it looks like at least that's going to be coming really down to the wire. So it just shows that there's different possibilities, which will also kind of shape how they govern, what kind of map they want to optimize towards in subsequent elections, which may just change the agenda to some degree.
turns.zh: 中西部除外。我记得 Bob Dole 说过一句话，大意是：农业州比其他任何类型的州都多得多，而这些州的分量永远更重。我觉得这对权力接下来怎么被塑造有影响。对民主党来说，还有一种感觉是'哦，原来这是可能的'。我不觉得民主党预期能赢 South Carolina，除非他们身在 Annie Andrews 那个竞选团队里。我也不觉得他们预期能赢 Mississippi，看起来至少 Mississippi 会咬到最后一刻。所以这就展示了不同的可能性，也会影响他们怎么执政、后续选举他们想优化到什么样的版图，这在某种程度上可能改变议程。

turns.en: Okay. So the Senate is important, but I think the consensus assumption is still there's going to be some form of political gridlock because, for instance, the Democrats don't have the 60 votes they need to push through a Republican filibuster and stuff like that. On the other hand, I think if we learned anything from Tuesday's elections, it's that Trump seems to be politically toxic now on both the Republican and the Democratic side. So maybe there's a potential to come together on like a few.
turns.zh: 好。所以参议院很重要，但我觉得主流的假设还是会出现某种形式的政治僵局，比如说，民主党没有 60 票来突破共和党的 filibuster（拖延战术）等等。另一方面，我觉得如果周二选举让我们学到什么，那就是 Trump 现在在共和党和民主党两边都算是政治毒药。所以也许在少数议题上有合作的可能。

turns.en: Issues at least. Yes, it's not. In general, divided government tends to be gridlock, right? So I think it means it's harder to pass policy. It becomes harder to pass policy in a crisis. So if you think about it, like we're talking about this in 2018, right? We were talking about, OK, there was the midterms effect, but Trump was kind of going forward with his kind of trade war, trade conflict issues. Fast forward 18 months later, and you have sort of the CARES Act issues from COVID. It just required a lot of coordination. Kind of worked out then in terms of at least Congress passed a lot of different things. I'm not sure how it's going to play out this time, right? Because it does seem like there's clearly, I said, the president's quite toxic. How polarizes it? Are Republicans willing to peel off? One thing that stood out from this election cycle was you could point to two very tangible things where Policy really did matter, right? You could say tariffs clearly identifiably moved prices and the war clearly had an effect. How that does, do any Republicans actually change their sort of approach to the president? I suspect that it's hard in the context of war to change a sort of executive action. Tariffs are more interesting because you're talking, we're talking about ag states. They're probably the ones who really like really holding the bag in terms of the cost of tariffs and sort of how they were executed by the president.
turns.zh: 至少在某些议题上。是的，这不是……一般来说，分立政府（divided government）往往导致僵局，对吧？所以我觉得这意味着政策更难通过。在危机中通过政策会更难。想想看，我们在 2018 年也是这样聊的，对吧？我们说'好，中期选举有影响，但 Trump 还在推进他的贸易战、贸易冲突'。18 个月后，你就有了新冠时期的 CARES Act 问题。那时候需要大量的协调。当时至少在国会通过了很多东西，还算过得去。我不确定这次会怎么演，对吧？因为看起来很明显，我说过总统在政治上很有毒。 polarize（极化）程度这么高，共和党愿不愿意脱离出来？这轮选举周期里有一点很突出：你可以指出两个非常实在的东西——政策真的起了作用，对吧？你可以说关税明确可辨识地推动了物价，战争也明确产生了影响。那共和党会不会真的改变他们对总统的态度？我猜在战争背景下改变行政行动是很难的。关税更有意思，因为我们谈的是农业州。他们大概率是真的在承担关税成本的那个群体，包括总统执行关税的方式。

turns.en: But tariffs are being pushed through now purely by executive order. So how much power does anyone else have to change them?
turns.zh: 但关税现在完全是靠行政令推进的。所以其他人还有多大权力去改变它？

turns.en: And the question is, are there Republicans in the ag states? There's still plenty of them, right? And I'm talking about the middle of the country, west of the Mississippi, who clearly, I mean, I don't think John Thune really likes aggressive tariffs. It has a lot of costs for farmers and for the ag industry. Are you able to peel off some of those to actually work on restricting sort of how much power the executive branch has over trade policy? These are all, again, they're all quite reaches because it's going to require pulling off an additional set of Republicans to work with Democrats and work against the president. That's, again, I'd say more tail scenario considerations. I'm sure Democrats will be happy to run on the idea that the president is raising costs through tariffs. But, I mean, if you think about where policy can change, it would require quite a substantial amount of coordination with other Republicans in the Senate.
turns.zh: 问题是，农业州还有共和党人吗？还有很多，对吧？我说的是密西西比河以西的美国中部地区。我觉得 John Thune 并不真的喜欢激进的关税。这对农民和农业有很多成本。你能不能把其中一些人拉出来，真正限制行政部门在贸易政策上的权力？当然这些都是很勉强的推演，因为这需要再拉一批共和党人来跟民主党合作、跟总统作对。这也是我说的尾部情景（tail scenario）考量。我确信民主党会很乐意拿'总统用关税抬高成本'这个说法去竞选。但如果你想想政策能在哪里改变，这需要跟参议院里其他共和党人做相当大量的协调。

turns.en: Just from a numbers thing, I mean... I was in a chat with you on Tuesday night and you're like, this is historic. Like what was the early on thing? You're like, oh, this is like, we're actually talking about a history making election.
turns.zh: 就从数字角度讲，我是说……周二晚上我在跟你聊天，你说'这是历史性的'。一开始你说什么来着？你说'哦，我们真的在讨论一场创造历史的选举'。

turns.en: Yeah. I think when you get early returns, the thing you want to look for is county comparisons where you actually have all the vote in, not just the early vote, because who votes early changes the cycle to cycle. But when you actually get those like first few counties that whether it's in Florida or Kentucky or Indiana. And you were seeing in some cases, obviously the Florida, some of the swings were narrower relative to 2024, something closer to five to eight points. But then you saw like outlier changes in a lot of other counties where it was closer to 20 points. And then it was okay. If it's 20 point swing from 2024 to 2026 in the same house race. Yeah. Those might be outliers, but it's telling you like, this is the distribution, right? And that distribution is there's like a long tail of outliers on them side. You're going to see like pretty big swings. In the end, what Texas, it seems like it's going to be close to double digits for. I've said it, but, you.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得拿到早期结果时，你要找的是那些所有选票都已经开完的县的对比，不只看提前投票，因为谁提前投票是每个周期都在变的。但当你真的拿到那最早几个县的数据——不管是 Florida、Kentucky 还是 Indiana——你会看到，在某些情况下，显然 Florida 的一些摇摆幅度相对 2024 变窄了，大概接近 5 到 8 个百分点。但你在很多其他县看到了异常变化，接近 20 个百分点。然后就变成：'如果是同一个众议院选区从 2024 到 2026 有 20 个百分点的摇摆……'是啊，这些可能是异常值，但它在告诉你分布是什么样的，对吧？这个分布就是：民主党方向上有一条长长的异常值尾巴，你会看到相当大的摇摆。最终在 Texas，看起来会接近两位数摇摆。我说过了，但你……

turns.en: Know, I've known a lot of people who work in Texas politics and they had like dream of like, well, maybe Texas will be a purple state one day. Oh, I see you wore a purple sweater today, by the way. Very bipartisan. No, no, like, and I used to just make fun of those people. That was so naive. And then to wake up, and I know so many, and it's like, it's not even a purple state. It's like a deep blue state now. I mean, the scale, it's a, what's that bomb where people, the new, like, A neutron bomb?
turns.zh: 你知道，我认识很多在 Texas 政坛工作的人，他们过去梦想着'也许有一天 Texas 会变成紫色州'。哦，顺便说一句，我看到你今天穿了件紫色毛衣，很两党嘛。不，我是说，我以前总是笑话那些人，说他们太天真了。然后一觉醒来，我认识这么多人，感觉是——它甚至都不是紫色州，现在是深蓝州了。我是说，那个规模，就像那种什么炸弹来着，那种新的，像中子弹（neutron bomb）？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: Where there's not even any destruction. It just, the people just disappear. It's everyone.
turns.zh: 就是那种连破坏都没有的，人就直接消失了。就是所有人。

turns.en: It's like, and it's also not just the things that you hear about. It's like the comptroller, the lieutenant governor.
turns.zh: 就像，而且不只是你听到的那些职位。是像审计长（comptroller）、副州长（lieutenant governor）。

turns.en: The education board. They're going to like change the University of Texas regents because someone just told me like that person's coming out for retirement and Hinojosa is going to get to work. appoint his replacement. Like the entire state in one night essentially goes like hard party rule. Like no one like, look, I know like the purple Texas stuff has been like for years. But now it's like you wake up one morning and Texas is not just like, at least for two years, it's not just like a blue state, but like a hardcore. It's really weird. Like everyone is just like, this is like a very surreal thing to see.
turns.zh: 教育委员会。他们要换掉 University of Texas 的理事，因为有人刚告诉我那个人要退休了，Hinojosa 就可以任命他的继任者。基本上整个州一夜之间就变成了强硬的政党统治。没人……我是说，我知道'紫色 Texas'的说法已经好多年了。但现在你一觉醒来，Texas 不仅是蓝州——至少接下来两年是——而且是硬核蓝州。这真的很奇怪。所有人都在说，这是非常超现实的景象。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think that the scale of the victory itself points to, there's just like newer possibilities in a lot of these states. And when you kind of think about Texas, when I think about what the business class sort of corporate America tends to tout certain states is like, this is the state you want to be. And, like, obviously it was Texas for a long time. Wait, tell us about this business court in Texas. No, this is important.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得胜利的规模本身就指向了这些州里更新的可能性。想到 Texas——当我想到商界、corporate America 一直鼓吹某些州是'你该去的地方'，显然长期以来那就是 Texas。等等，跟我们说说 Texas 的这个商事法庭（business court）。不，这个很重要。

turns.en: We'll have to do a separate episode.
turns.zh: 我们得单独做一期。

turns.en: I think you'll probably need to get a separate episode.
turns.zh: 我觉得你们可能真的需要单独做一期。

turns.en: What's the story here?

turns.en: I suspect what will matter most there is economics more than the politics. And I do think that we were seeing, we're definitely seeing whispers and whiffs of this before the election itself. Oh, there's like, markets aren't always rewarding more CapEx. How useful is this? Oh, now we start to see the S1 from Anthropic. We haven't yet seen that on OpenAI. It's like, this is a lot of investment. It's a lot of risk. Do we just kind of keep greenlighting it because it's progressing the frontier? Or is there actually like, because CapEx is also a burden. So I think we're seeing some of that, some of the rewarding of capital efficiency over just raw CapEx. Nevertheless, I feel like this is going to be a bit of a sea change in terms of the politics now where, yeah, look, if you take five or six governors and they all are of the same party, could presumably even coordinate their own efforts if they really wanted to. That sort of changes how easy it is to do business For a long time, even in a lot of blue states, there were like a lot of tax breaks for data centers. And it was sort of seen as like, oh, we want to invite this economic activity. It's very good. And at least for the past 12 months, it got super toxic in terms of politically. That might not be the case going forward, or at least there may be a better path ahead. But yeah, clearly there are new variables for a lot of the hyperscalers, a lot of sort of the companies that are really kind of leading this sort of construction effort to kind of grapple with that they did not have to deal with before. Josh Shapiro and Greg Abbott probably two of the most pro-data center governors I can probably point to. I think they both made pivots, and Josh Shapiro seems to have pulled off the pivot very successfully, Greg Abbott less so. That might just be a function of the macro environment more than data center messaging in any way. But I think it's quite telling, right? That even those who are the most favorable towards this type of activity have had to read the room, recognize that things have to change, at least to manage the electoral cycle. And I think the question from here is, is there an ability to rebrand any of this stuff, or will there just be a focus on Maybe we don't need to have such a heavy footprint. We can find other ways to kind of do what we need to do without attracting so much nimbyism or any kind of like specific detractors in political space.
turns.zh: 我猜在那里最重要的其实是经济因素，而不是政治。我确实觉得，在选举之前我们就已经看到、听到一些风声了。'哦，市场不再总是奖励更多的资本开支（CapEx）。这些钱花得有多值？'现在我们看到了 Anthropic 的 S-1，OpenAI 那边还没看到。'这是大量的投资，也是大量的风险。我们要不要在推进前沿的名义下继续开绿灯？还是……'因为 CapEx 也是一种负担。所以我觉得我们看到了一些这样的东西，看到资本效率开始被奖励，而不只是纯粹的 CapEx。尽管如此，我觉得政治层面上这算是一次不小的转变。是的，你看，如果你有五六个州长都是同一个党的，他们甚至可以真的协调自己的行动，如果他们真想这么做的话。这就改变了做生意的难易程度。长期以来，甚至在很多蓝州，数据中心都能拿到很多税收优惠。大家觉得'哦，我们要吸引这种经济活动，这很好'。至少在过去 12 个月里，这在政治上变得超级有毒。未来可能不是这样，或者至少可能有一条更好的路。但显然，对那些超大规模云厂商（hyperscalers）、那些真正在 leading 这波建设的公司来说，出现了他们以前不必面对的新变量。Josh Shapiro 和 Greg Abbott 大概是我能指出来的最支持数据中心的两位州长。我觉得他们都做了转向，Josh Shapiro 似乎转向得非常成功，Greg Abbott 就没那么成功。这可能更多是宏观环境的作用，而不完全是数据中心信息传达的问题。但我觉得这很能说明问题，对吧？即便那些对这类活动最友好的人，也不得不读一下风向、承认事情必须改变，至少是为了应付选举周期。我觉得接下来的问题是：他们能不能把这些东西重新包装？还是会转向'也许我们不需要那么重的落地 footprint，我们可以找其他方式来做我们要做的事，而不会招来那么多的邻避主义（NIMBYism）或者政治空间里的具体反对者'。

turns.en: Yeah, part of that is a rates move. And so you have just a, there's clearly some effect of if you have less AI CapEx, you will have maybe a softer economy, lower interest rates. There's more room for other things to thrive. I'm quite skeptical that if you did see AI CapEx really cool off, these things tend to not be very linear. It tends to be more binary. It's on or off. And once it's off, is there something that's going to pick up that slack very quickly? That's obviously the Goldilocks outcome. Yeah, I'd say history suggests that's hard to pull off. So we are obviously in a world where I'd still characterize it as an AI boom. I'd still say there's obviously a lot of activity going on. There's a lot of activity still booked to happen. But if the tide comes out, I'm not as convinced that there is going to be some big housing boom that offsets it. So another set of... Those things take time to really get going as well. So you don't have this super nice sort of counter-cyclicality here in terms of how the economy works. And so you have the share of what I call the AI-sensitive segments of spending in the kind of GDP mix have grown at such an enormous pace. It's something getting close to 8% of GDP if I think about just your tech hardware, tech software, and industrial equipment. Those categories itself make up such a large share of the U.S. economy. From the demand side, obviously a lot of it is imported, but it still matters. This is still like spending. Spending is a risk. Someone who is spending is putting that on their income statement, their balance sheet in the U.S. And so these dynamics are probably going to dictate the cycle. I think that's not actually at this point very original to say, but we have coming into this year, there's a sense of, oh, the non-AI economy is soft. It's like, I'm not sure that's quite true. It's like not amazing. The other side is inflation, right, where we have three themes, maybe four at this point, that are going to matter. Look, the Strait of Hormuz closure and to some degree, obviously, some of the refining capacity issues that are maybe tied also to the Russia-Ukraine conflict have clearly blown out sort of set of prices for jet fuel. And that has pushed up airfares quite considerably. So when people are saying, ah, well, services inflation is running hot, it's like because airfares are sensitive to energy. It's not necessarily because of the labor market. diesel prices are very high. Caught a lot of political attention, but the effects actually on the consumer have yet to be seen really, which is to say like there's a lot of, I'm curious for a lot of the food retailers who have had to take on additional energy costs and transport costs. Are they going to have to pass through higher prices than the food, food services inflation, which actually does matter for core. That energy dynamic is clearly one big thing that I think, I suspect we're still kind of processing. It may not, be more aggressive in the next several months, but it may be called just as aggressive or pretty close to what we've seen in the last several months. Then you have the AI boom itself, where it's still places where this is showing up. Again, maybe we're past the peak impulse, but it may be more durable than people realize in terms of we had a lot of prices that spiked for your laptops, for various sort of things tied to memory, but there's still more things that could rise. So that might just mean that we had to deal with more durable inflation there. And the third piece of this is obviously tariffs itself. Look, there are a lot of categories that have already moved. There are some categories, notable categories that have not moved yet. Cars, right? Like you have not seen anything that's happened in the auto space. And some of that is because it's a different tariff regime there. But even so, there were a lot of the Canadian tariffs that were put on and on off that still cost that's not yet passed through to the consumer. And so I think those three themes are still with us. It may not mean that we're going to go to 4% inflation, but we might be stuck around three a lot longer than is currently suspected.
turns.zh: 对，其中一部分是利率的变动。所以你就有了——很明显，如果 AI CapEx 减少，经济可能会更软、利率会更低，其他东西就有更多空间繁荣起来。我很怀疑——如果你真的看到 AI CapEx 明显降温——这些东西往往不是线性的，往往更二元化：要么开要么关。一旦关掉，有什么东西能很快接上那个空缺吗？那显然就是 Goldilocks（金发姑娘）结果。是的，我会说历史表明这很难实现。所以我们显然还在一个我依然会称之为 AI 繁荣的世界里。我依然觉得显然有大量活动在发生，还有大量已经预定要发生的活动。但如果潮水退了，我不太确信会出现一个大的房地产繁荣来抵消。所以另一组……这些东西要真的启动起来也需要时间。所以你在经济运作上并没有那种非常漂亮的反周期性。所以我所说的 AI 敏感支出部分在 GDP 结构中的份额以极快的速度增长。仅仅考虑科技硬件、科技软件和工业设备这几项，就接近 GDP 的 8%。这些类别本身在美国经济中占据了如此大的份额。从需求侧看，显然很多是进口的，但它依然重要。这仍然是支出。支出是一种风险。花钱的人会把它记在自己的损益表和资产负债表上，在美国境内。所以这些动态大概率会主导这轮周期。我觉得这个说法现在已经不算很原创了，但今年年初进来的时候，大家有一种感觉'哦，非 AI 经济疲软'。我不确定这是否完全成立，就是不算惊艳。另一方面是通胀，对吧？我们有三个主题——也许是四个——会重要。看，霍尔木兹海峡（Strait of Hormuz）的关闭，以及在某种程度上显然与俄乌冲突相关的一些炼油产能问题，已经明显推高了一组价格，比如航空燃油。这就把机票价格推得相当高。所以当人们说'啊，服务通胀在升温'，那是因为机票对能源敏感，不一定是因为劳动力市场。柴油价格非常高，引起了很多政治关注，但对消费者的实际影响其实还没真的显现——也就是说，我很好奇很多不得不吸收额外能源成本和运输成本的食品零售商，他们会不会不得不转嫁更高的价格。食品服务通胀，这个对核心 CPI 确实有影响。这个能源动态显然是一个大主题，我猜我们还在消化。接下来几个月它可能不会更激进，但可能会跟过去几个月一样激进或者接近。然后是 AI 繁荣本身，仍在一些地方显现。也许我们已经过了峰值冲动，但可能比人们意识到的更持久——我们有很多价格飙升，比如笔记本电脑、各种跟内存相关的东西，但还有更多东西可能会涨。所以这可能意味着我们要应对更持久的通胀。第三块显然就是关税本身。看，很多类别已经动了。有一些重要类别还没动。汽车，对吧？你在汽车这块什么都还没看到。部分原因是那里的关税机制不一样。但即便如此，很多加拿大关税被反复开关，成本还没传导到消费者。所以我觉得这三个主题依然伴随我们。这不意味着我们会去到 4% 的通胀，但我们可能在 3% 附近卡住的时间比现在大家猜测的要长得多。
